analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 income tax cuts permanent and sets the estate tax at 35% with a $5 million exemption.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2010 with 27 Republican cosponsors, it was placed on the Senate calendar the next day and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the expiration dates written into the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, making all of those tax cuts permanent — including the lower top income tax rates and the low 15% rates on capital gains and dividends. It would also permanently patch the alternative minimum tax so millions of households don't get pulled into it, keep the expanded child tax credit and marriage penalty relief, and write a new estate tax into permanent law: 35% on estates above $5 million per person, with a spouse able to use their deceased husband's or wife's unused $5 million exemption. The bill was introduced by the Senate Republican leader, never scheduled for a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: the bill makes the lower top income tax brackets, the 15% capital gains and dividends rates, and the related provisions permanent rather than letting them lapse at the end of 2010. Heirs to large estates gain from a permanent 35% estate tax with a $5 million exclusion — far below the pre-2001 tax — plus the ability of a surviving spouse to add their deceased spouse's unused exemption, shielding up to $10 million per couple. Middle- and upper-middle-income households also gain from the permanent alternative minimum tax fix, the retained child tax credit, and marriage penalty relief.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and heirs of large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the December 31, 2010 sunset on the 2001 tax law's provisions and the 2003 law's capital gains and dividend rate cuts, making them permanent [S2].

Writes a permanent alternative minimum tax exemption — $72,450 for joint filers in 2010, rising to about $110,000 by 2020 — so households with children and state tax deductions are not pulled into the AMT [S3].
Restores marriage penalty relief and the increased child tax credit on a permanent basis [S2].

Sets a permanent estate tax of 35% on amounts above a $5 million exclusion, lets a surviving spouse use the deceased spouse's unused exclusion, and gives 2010 estates a choice of tax regimes [S2, S3].
Expands the tax credits that can offset the alternative minimum tax, including credits for adoption, children, home mortgages, residential energy property, and plug-in electric vehicles [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue. Because the bill makes the tax cuts permanent with no offsetting revenue in the text, the difference is carried by future federal borrowing. The largest share of the added cost of extending all of the cuts, rather than extending only the middle-class portions, comes from the provisions that benefit the top brackets, capital gains and dividends, and large estates.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offsets: it repeals the sunset dates on the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts outright, locking in the revenue loss permanently rather than funding any of it [S3].

Its estate tax terms — a 35% rate and a $5 million exclusion with spousal portability — shield estates up to roughly $10 million per couple from any federal estate tax, a benefit available only to the largest estates; the pre-2001 law taxed estates above $1 million at up to 55% [S2, S3].

The honest cost of the middle-class pieces — the AMT fix, the child tax credit, marriage penalty relief — is real but smaller; the added cost of making the top-bracket and investment-rate cuts permanent falls overwhelmingly on high-income households and on the deficit [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The middle-class and AMT provisions are genuinely valuable — without them, millions of households would have faced higher bills and an expanding AMT. But the bill bundles those with its most expensive provisions, the permanent top-rate cuts and the deeply reduced estate tax, which accrue mostly to the wealthiest households and add to deficits without any pay-for. A narrower bill extending only the middle-class provisions would have captured most of the benefit for ordinary families at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and placed on the Senate calendar two days later, but no senator ever brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on September 13, 2010, joined by 24 Senate Republicans including Grassley, Kyl, McCain, and Hatch [S3].
Twenty-seven Senate Republicans — 27 of the chamber's 40 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did [S4].

On September 14, 2010, it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 562, which is where bills wait to be brought up for floor action [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no motion to proceed. The Congress ended January 3, 2011, with the bill still sitting on the calendar [S5].

The bill's title and text present the full extension as preventing tax hikes, framing the December 31, 2010 expiration of the 2001 and 2003 provisions as a tax increase on taxpayers at every income level [S2, S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death meant the wealthiest households and large estates did not get the permanent rate cuts and the $5 million, 35% estate tax this bill would have locked in through this vehicle; the debate instead moved to separate two-year extension legislation later that December.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Its beneficiaries got no permanence from this bill

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make all of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and to write in a 35%/$5 million estate tax.

for.name: 27 of 40 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it the Senate Republicans' vehicle for the full extension of the Bush-era tax cuts.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.role: The chamber's 58-seat Democratic majority controlled the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it sat on the legislative calendar from September 14, 2010 until the Congress ended with no vote scheduled.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: The Democratic leader who controls which calendar bills come to the floor never brought this bill up for a vote; his party favored extending only the middle-class portions of the cuts.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Republican — 27 of the chamber's 40 — and no Democrat signed on; the Democratic majority that controlled the floor never scheduled it for a vote.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: The bill makes the top income tax rates and the 15% capital gains and dividends rates permanent and caps the estate tax at 35% with a $5 million exclusion plus spousal portability. The revenue foregone on these provisions is the bill's largest cost, borne by federal taxpayers collectively.
The permanent AMT exemption — shielding joint filers up to roughly $110,000 by 2020 — plus the child tax credit and marriage penalty relief directly reduce taxes for millions of working households.

industries.industry: Clean energy and auto industries (electric vehicles, residential energy systems)
industries.note: The bill rewrites the rules so credits for plug-in electric vehicles and residential energy property can offset the AMT and carry forward, making those credits more usable for buyers of solar, geothermal, and electric-vehicle products.

industries.industry: Home building, real estate, and mortgage finance
industries.note: The mortgage interest credit and residential rehabilitation provisions are made usable against the AMT, and the first-time homebuyer credit for District of Columbia buyers gets a carryforward rule, modestly supporting home purchase and renovation.
